title: Given the root of a binary tree, imagine standing on the left side of it; return the values of the nodes visible from the left, ordered top to bottom. This is the first node of each level in a level order traversal.
shortTitle: Left View of a Binary Tree (First Node of Each Level)
keyPoints: The left view is the first node of each level in a BFS, not just the left spine of the tree
Use the level-size snapshot and capture the node when index equals 0
A right-child node can appear in the left view if the left subtree does not extend to that depth
The DFS alternative visits left before right and records the first node at each new depth
This is the mirror of the right view: change the capture index from last to first
Time is O(n), space is O(w) for BFS or O(h) for DFS

s1_definition.oneliner: BFS per level; capture the first node of each level into the result.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Left view** – the mirror of the right view: the first node of each level, top to bottom.
- **Level-size snapshot** – capture `queue.size()` at each level's start, drain that many nodes, and record the first (index == 0).
- **Not the left spine** – the leftmost node per level may come from the right subtree if the left subtree is shorter.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(w) space for BFS; O(n) time, O(h) space for DFS.
- **Symmetric** – the right view captures the last node per level.
s1_definition.analogy: Looking at the National Bank of India approval tree from the left edge, you see only the leftmost approver on each rank, because they stand in front of everyone to their right. Collecting the leftmost approver per rank top to bottom is the left view.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  BFS Left View

       CEO          Level 0: first = CEO
      /   \
    VP1   VP2       Level 1: first = VP1
           \
           DIR2     Level 2: first = DIR2

  Left view: [CEO, VP1, DIR2]
  Note: DIR2 is a right child but leftmost at level 2
```

```text
  DFS Left-First Visit Order

  Visit: CEO(0) → VP1(1) → VP2(1,skip) → DIR2(2)
  Result builds: [CEO] → [CEO,VP1] → [CEO,VP1,DIR2]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The left view of a binary tree is the mirror of the right view: it is the first node of each level, top to bottom. You compute it with the same BFS level-size snapshot, but capture the node at index 0 instead of `levelSize - 1`. Children are enqueued left then right as in every BFS variant.

The key insight is the same as for the right view: the left view is defined per level, not per branch. Following only left children fails when the right subtree runs deeper. The first-index rule captures the correct node regardless of which subtree it comes from.

The DFS alternative visits left before right and records the first node at each new depth. Both BFS and DFS are O(n) time; BFS uses O(w) space and DFS uses O(h) space.

In our banking system at National Bank of India, the left view produces an entry-point summary showing the first approver reachable at each escalation rank. Presenting the left and right views together as the symmetric first-node and last-node rules shows command of the whole Tree BFS family.

Remember one sentence: BFS level-size snapshot, capture the first node per level; that is the left view, the mirror of the right view.
